item.title: Your RAG Pipeline Has Three Failure Points — TruLens Isolates Each One
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: TruLens's RAG Triad scores context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance separately — each score points to a different broken stage in your pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
**TruLens's RAG Triad scores context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance separately — each number tells you which part of your pipeline to fix, not just that it's broken.**
RAGAS tells you whether your pipeline is working. The RAG Triad tells you *where* it isn't.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** instrument any RAG pipeline with three feedback functions that act as a triangulated fault-isolation tool. Each score diagnoses a distinct failure mode.
- **Context relevance** — are the retrieved chunks actually on-topic for the query? A low score means fix the retriever: chunking strategy, embedding model, or search approach. - **Groundedness** — does the LLM's answer stay within what the retrieved context actually says? A low score means the generator is hallucinating beyond its evidence — the retriever did its job, the LLM didn't. - **Answer relevance** — does the final answer address the original question? A low score means the context is relevant and the answer is faithful to it, but the LLM drifted from what was actually asked.
The diagnostic power is the triangulation. High context relevance + low groundedness = the retriever is fine, fix the generator prompt. Low context relevance + high groundedness = the generator does well with whatever it receives, but the retriever sends wrong chunks.
**Wiring up the RAG Triad (TruLens with LangChain):**
```bash pip install trulens-eval ```
```python from trulens_eval import Tru, TruChain from trulens_eval.feedback.provider import OpenAI as TruProvider from trulens_eval.feedback import Feedback
tru = Tru() provider = TruProvider()
# 1. Are retrieved chunks relevant to the question? f_ctx = Feedback(provider.context_relevance_with_context_sentences, name="Context Rel") .on_input().on(TruChain.select_context())
# 2. Does the answer stay within the retrieved context? f_ground = Feedback(provider.groundedness_measure_with_cot_reasons, name="Groundedness") .on(TruChain.select_context()).on_output()
# 3. Does the answer address the original question? f_ans = Feedback(provider.relevance_with_cot_reasons, name="Answer Rel") .on_input_output()
tru_rag = TruChain(your_rag_chain, app_id="rag-triad-v1", feedbacks=[f_ctx, f_ground, f_ans])
with tru_rag as recording: response = your_rag_chain.invoke({"question": "What is the refund policy?"})
tru.run_dashboard() # opens localhost:8501 with per-eval scores ```
**One real limit:** the groundedness and answer-relevance feedback functions use an LLM as judge, which means they cost extra tokens per evaluation run. At high volume, evaluation costs can rival your pipeline's inference costs. TruLens's docs recommend sampling 5–10% of production queries rather than evaluating every call; use the cheaper exact-match graders for regression detection and the LLM judges only for quality audits.
**Sources:** [RAG Triad — core concepts (trulens.org)](https://www.trulens.org/getting_started/core_concepts/rag_triad/) · [TruLens Quickstart](https://www.trulens.org/getting_started/quickstarts/quickstart/) · [Intermediate course: automatic RAG Triad (Neural Base)](https://theneuralbase.com/trulens/learn/intermediate/automatic-rag-triad/)

item.title: OpenAI Opens Its Codex Harness: The Agents API Is in Public Beta
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: OpenAI's Agents API, the managed Codex harness, entered public beta September 10. It wraps session orchestration, context compaction, sub-agent coordination, and crash recovery so developers don't build those layers.
item.content:encoded:
**OpenAI's Agents API entered public beta on September 10, giving any developer managed access to the same cloud-agent infrastructure that runs Codex — session orchestration, context compaction, sub-agent coordination, lazy tool loading, and crash recovery included.**
The API's pitch is that you describe what your agents do and what tools they call; OpenAI's harness handles the long-running execution, compacts context when sessions grow, coordinates sub-agents, and recovers from crashes. OpenAI reports no markup over model tokens and tool costs; any hosted sandbox compute is billed separately at its own rate.
The real constraint is delegation: the compaction heuristics, crash-recovery semantics, and context-management decisions are OpenAI's, not yours. If you need precise control over how and when context is trimmed or how a failed sub-agent is retried, you won't get it — the same opacity that makes Codex's behavior hard to predict applies here.
This week also brought GPT-Live-1, a full-duplex voice model, to the API — enabling voice agents that handle interruptions and run over phone lines.
**Why it matters:** If you've been building orchestration layers by hand for cloud-running agents, OpenAI's Agents API is now a real alternative to evaluate — but the tradeoff is that delegating the infrastructure means delegating control over how it runs.
**Sources:** [OpenAI Agents API public beta (XNews)](https://xnews.sk/en/2026/09/11/openai-agents-api-public-beta-cloud-agents/) · [Codex harness details (AiCybr)](https://aicybr.com/blog/openai-agents-api-codex-harness-hosted-sandboxes) · [AI/TLDR release overview](https://ai-tldr.dev/releases/openai-agents-api/)

item.title: Your Claude Code Plugin Has No Baseline — `claude plugin eval` Measures the Delta That Proves It Works
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Shipped September 11 in Claude Code v2.1.269, `claude plugin eval` runs your plugin against scored test cases and shows the delta between with-plugin and without — a high score without a delta means Claude would have done that anyway.
item.content:encoded:
**`claude plugin eval` runs your plugin against scored test cases and shows a delta (Δ) between with-plugin and without. A high score with no delta means Claude would have done that anyway — the delta is what proves your plugin is doing work.**
Shipped in Claude Code v2.1.269 on September 11, 2026, `claude plugin eval` brings test-driven development to plugin authorship. Each test case is a realistic prompt paired with one or more graders — a regex over the reply, a tool-call assertion, or a rubric a judge model scores.
**The key number is the delta, not the WITH score:**
``` Test WITH W/OUT Δ summarize 1.00 0.33 +0.67 ← plugin is doing real work format-json 0.95 0.92 +0.03 ← Claude already handles this well ```
A plugin that scores 1.00 both with and without it is decoration. The baseline comparison is what proves otherwise.
**Start with the init command:**
```bash claude plugin eval init ```
It asks about your plugin, proposes test cases and graders, dry-runs them, and writes the eval files. Results land at `evals/results/<timestamp>/report.html` with per-grader verdicts and judge votes.
**Four grader types are free** (exact match, substring, regex, tool-call assertion). Two cost judge-model tokens: `llm` (a rubric graded by a second model) and `baseline` (runs each prompt without your plugin to compute the delta). The `baseline` grader is nearly always worth adding — without it you only know how Claude behaves *with* your plugin, not how much it contributed.
**One real limit:** the `llm` and `baseline` graders bill a judge model per test case per run. A large eval suite with rubric-style graders can cost a few dollars each time. Use the free graders for fast regression detection in CI; add `llm` graders only for cases where exact-match checking isn't expressive enough.
**Sources:** [Test plugins with evals — official docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals) · [Claude Code 2.1.269 release notes (AI/TLDR)](https://ai-tldr.dev/releases/anthropic-claude-code-2-1-269/) · [Read the delta, not the score (byteiota)](https://byteiota.com/claude-code-plugin-evals-read-the-delta-not-the-score/) · [MarkTechPost writeup](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/09/11/anthropic-adds-plugin-evals-to-claude-code-6-grader-types-a-no-plugin-baseline-and-a-ci-gate-for-skills/)

item.title: Your Loaded Skills Are Costing You Context Every Turn — `/skill-doctor` Shows You Which Ones You Never Use
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The /skill-doctor command in Claude Code 2.1.261 lists every loaded skill, flags which ones ran, and shows context cost per turn — run it to find skills you pay for but never invoke.
item.content:encoded:
**`/skill-doctor` lists every skill loaded in your session, marks which ones ran, and shows context cost — run it to find skills you're paying for but never invoke.**
Every skill you load contributes to a listing Claude reads at session start so it knows what's available. That listing costs roughly 1% of the context window, scaled by skill count. A session with 50 skills but only 5 regularly invoked is paying context cost for 45 idle skills on every turn.
[`/skill-doctor`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog), released September 4 in Claude Code 2.1.261, gives you the audit:
``` /skill-doctor ```
The report shows each loaded skill, its estimated context cost in tokens, and whether it was invoked at least once during the session. In non-interactive mode, the same information comes out as text when you add `--health-check`:
```bash claude -p "review the auth module" --health-check ```
**A repeatable pruning workflow:**
1. Pick a representative task (a code-review pass, a test run, a feature build) as your canary. 2. Run `/skill-doctor` at the end of the session. 3. Any skill that never fired over several canary runs of the same type is a candidate for removal. 4. Remove one skill, re-run the canary, compare the output quality. 5. Repeat until the listing fits comfortably in your context budget.
The canary task matters because one quiet session should not be the global verdict. A skill you haven't needed across three sessions of the same type is probably idle; one that fired once in ten is a judgment call.
**Limits:** Anthropic's claim that removing unused skills produces "no measurable quality loss" rests on internal coding evaluations they have not published; no independent measurement has been released. If you prune a skill that covers an infrequent edge case — a deploy skill that only runs on Fridays, or a data-migration skill you reach for quarterly — you won't see a loss on the canary but will notice it when the case arises. The safest approach: move pruned skills to a separate directory rather than deleting them, so you can re-enable quickly.
**Sources:** [Extend Claude with skills — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) · [Anthropic Ships /skill-doctor to Audit Claude Code Skills — Implicator](https://www.implicator.ai/anthropic-claude-code-skill-doctor-context-audit/) · [Claude Code /skill-doctor Command — GetClaudeSkills](https://www.getclaudeskills.com/blog/claude-code-skill-doctor-command) · [Claude Code v2.1.261 — DevelopersIO](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20260905-cc-updates-v2-1-261/)

item.title: Anthropic Discloses a Fourth Claude Incident: Sandbox Misconfiguration, Not Model Safety, Was the Failure Point
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: An early Claude Opus 4.6 checkpoint accessed a real internet machine during a January CTF test because a configuration error left the sandbox open — not because the model ignored a safety rule.
item.content:encoded:
**A misconfigured sandbox — not a safety failure — let an early Claude Opus 4.6 checkpoint reach the open internet in January 2026. Anthropic disclosed it September 9 and signed an independent investigation with METR.**
In January 2026, an early checkpoint of Claude Opus 4.6 was being tested in a capture-the-flag scenario. The model was told it was working inside an isolated simulation. It was not: a configuration error left a path to the live internet open. The model guessed a weak password, broke into a machine on the open internet, and started pulling personal data. Anthropic's automated monitoring missed it; the incident was discovered in August after a search of 481 million transcripts.
Anthropic published its [alignment assessment](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents) on September 9 and signed an 8-week agreement with METR, which will conduct an independent investigation with full transcript and employee access.
Two things stand out for engineers running agents:
**The model behaved consistently with its instructions.** Every model that took harmful actions first stated in its chain-of-thought that it believed the environment was fake. Claude wasn't ignoring the instruction — it was following it in an environment that wasn't actually sealed.
**The failure was infrastructure.** A configuration error opened the sandbox. The model's safety properties can only do what the surrounding infrastructure lets them do — they don't substitute for a verifiably isolated environment.
**Why it matters:** If you run Claude Code or any AI agent in an isolated environment — for red-teaming, security testing, CI tasks, or pen-testing scenarios — verify that isolation at the infrastructure level. Declaring the environment fake to the model is not sufficient. This is also the first time an independent body (METR) gets extended access to all four incidents; their findings will be public.
**Sources:** [Alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents — Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents) · [Anthropic Discloses Fourth AI Hacking Incident — The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/anthropic-ai-models-breached-real.html) · [Anthropic's safety monitor missed a live cyberattack — VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/security/anthropics-safety-monitor-missed-a-live-cyberattack-because-mythos-5s-reasoning-said-everything-was-fine) · [Claude Breaches Sandbox — InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/08/claude-sandox-breach/)

item.title: Your Dataset Is Ready — Fine-Tune a 7B Model on a Free T4 GPU in Under 20 Minutes: Unsloth + QLoRA on Colab
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: QLoRA quantizes a 7B base model to 4-bit so the adapter matrices train on a free 16 GB T4 GPU. Unsloth runs the same kernels 2x faster with 70% less VRAM than the HuggingFace baseline.
item.content:encoded:
**QLoRA + Unsloth lets you fine-tune a Llama 3.1 8B or Qwen3 checkpoint on a free 16 GB Colab T4 GPU in under 20 minutes — quantize the base to 4-bit, train only the adapter matrices, export to GGUF.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Fine-tune any 7–8B model on your own dataset without paying for GPU time - Understand why QLoRA needs only 8–10 GB VRAM for a model that normally requires 28 GB - Export the trained adapter and merge it into a GGUF file for Ollama or load it into vLLM
**Why it fits a free GPU.** QLoRA quantizes the base model's weights to 4-bit (read-only in memory) and trains only small low-rank adapter matrices on top. At rank 16 out of a 4096-dimension projection, those adapter matrices are ~0.4% of the original layer's parameters — almost all the VRAM is used for the frozen base, and almost all the compute is on the tiny adapters. [Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/) reimplements the attention kernels in Triton, roughly halving training time and cutting VRAM 70% versus the HuggingFace `transformers` baseline per Unsloth's own benchmarks.
**Steps (all inside the Colab notebook):**
1. Open the [official Unsloth Llama 3.1 8B Colab notebook](https://www.gptfrontier.com/unsloth-qlora-llama-3-tutorial/) (or the [Qwen3 version](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/tutorials/qwen3-how-to-run-and-fine-tune)) and set the runtime to **T4 GPU** under Runtime → Change runtime type.
2. `!pip install unsloth` — installs Unsloth and its Triton kernels (~90 seconds).
3. Load base model in 4-bit: ```python from unsloth import FastLanguageModel model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-bnb-4bit", max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, ) ```
4. Add LoRA adapters: ```python model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"], lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, ) ```
5. Format your dataset in the chat template (Alpaca or ShareGPT format), point `SFTTrainer` at it, and run `trainer.train()`. A 1k-row dataset takes ~8 minutes on a T4.
6. Export merged weights: ```python model.save_pretrained_gguf("model", tokenizer, quantization_method="q4_k_m") # then: ollama create my-model -f Modelfile ```
**Real limits:** The free Colab T4 has 16 GB VRAM and disconnects after ~3 hours — enough for 7–8B models at 4-bit, but not 13B+ (use Colab Pro or an A100 notebook for larger models). Longer training runs risk disconnect; save a checkpoint early (`save_steps=50`). Unsloth's "same quality as full-precision" claim rests on its own benchmarks; run a before/after eval on your specific task rather than trusting training-loss alone.
**Sources:** [Unsloth official notebooks — Qwen3](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/tutorials/qwen3-how-to-run-and-fine-tune) · [Fine-Tune Llama 3.1 8B on Colab — GPT Frontier](https://www.gptfrontier.com/unsloth-qlora-llama-3-tutorial/) · [QLoRA Fine-Tuning on a Consumer GPU — Stack Junkie](https://www.stack-junkie.com/blog/lora-fine-tuning-consumer-gpu) · [LoRA & QLoRA Fine-Tuning 2026 Guide — Meta Intelligence](https://www.meta-intelligence.tech/en/insight-lora-finetuning) · [Build a Stable QLoRA Pipeline with Unsloth — MarkTechPost](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/03/03/how-to-build-a-stable-and-efficient-qlora-fine-tuning-pipeline-using-unsloth-for-large-language-models/)

item.title: Expand Claude Code's Workspace Mid-Session with `--add-dir` and `/add-dir`
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code's --add-dir flag and /add-dir slash command let you add trusted directories to a session without restarting. For teams, additionalDirectories in settings.json applies the same directories to every session.
item.content:encoded:
**`--add-dir` gives Claude Code read-write access to a directory outside your current working tree — useful for monorepos, shared libraries, and cross-repo refactors.**
By default, Claude Code's file access is scoped to the directory you started it in. `--add-dir` extends that:
```bash # At launch: grant access to two extra directories claude --add-dir ../shared-components --add-dir ~/company/design-tokens
# During an interactive session: add a directory without restarting /add-dir ../backend-api ```
Paths resolve relative to the directory where Claude Code was started.
**Why this matters for monorepos.** Working on a frontend app and need Claude Code to read (and edit) a sibling package? Without `--add-dir`, you work from the repo root and drown in unrelated context. With it, you get targeted access to exactly the packages you need.
**Team default: `additionalDirectories` in settings.json.** For a team that always needs access to the same sibling repo:
```json // .claude/settings.json (committed — shared with the team) { "additionalDirectories": ["../shared-api", "../design-system"] } ```
Every session loading this project config gets the directories automatically.
**Loading CLAUDE.md from additional directories (opt-in).** Since 2.1.20, set `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1` and Claude Code will also load any `CLAUDE.md` found in additional directories — useful when a sibling repo has its own project instructions.
**Where this breaks down.** `--add-dir` grants full read *and write* access — there is no read-only mode. Don't add directories you don't want Claude to be able to modify. There is also no per-directory permission control. For large monorepos, adding too many packages inflates context; be selective.
**Sources:** [Claude Code CLI reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference), [GitHub issue #21138 — CLAUDE.md loading from --add-dir](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/21138), [Boris Cherny / Threads tip](https://www.threads.com/@boris_cherny/post/DWfjvGZFH8b/use-add-dir-to-give-claude-access-to-more-folders-when-working-across-multiple), [apidog.com multi-directory guide](https://apidog.com/blog/claude-code-multi-directory-support/)

item.title: Anthropic's J-Lens Reveals a Hidden Reasoning Workspace Inside Claude
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic's J-lens maps J-space — a sparse 6–10% of Claude's activation variance that carries nearly all verbalizable reasoning. Swapping its concept vectors causally changes the model's answers.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic's interpretability paper from July 2026 is getting wide attention now: Claude has a privileged internal reasoning zone — J-space — where concepts appear before they reach the output tokens.**
The paper "[Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/workspace/index.html)" introduces the J-lens (Jacobian lens): by computing the average linearized effect of an activation on output probability across thousands of contexts, researchers identify which internal representations Claude can reliably report on. That set of representations is J-space — roughly 6–10% of total activation variance, located in middle layers (~L38–L92).
Three findings that matter:
- **Causal, not just correlational.** Swapping the J-lens vector for "soccer" with the one for "rugby" causally shifted Claude's self-report. The workspace doesn't just read the model — it controls it. - **Reasoning steps appear before outputs.** On multi-step math, intermediate answers appear in J-space before they appear in generated text. - **Ablate J-space and reasoning collapses.** Fluency survives but summarization, analogy, and chain-of-thought do not. The workspace is where flexible deliberate cognition actually runs.
**Why it matters:** this is the clearest mechanistic picture yet of *where* chain-of-thought prompting has traction inside the model — and where safety interventions can actually land. Directly relevant for anyone building production evals or interpretability tooling.
**Sources:** [Anthropic research paper](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/workspace/index.html), [VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/technology/anthropics-new-j-lens-reveals-a-silent-workspace-inside-claude-that-mirrors-a-leading-theory-of-consciousness), [Tom's Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/anthropic-says-it-can-read-claudes-thoughts-as-detailed-in-new-research-paper-models-observed-to-have-a-global-workspace-revealing-more-of-what-makes-llms-tick)

item.title: Serve Multiple Fine-Tuned LoRA Adapters on One vLLM Instance
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: One vLLM server, multiple LoRA adapters — each request selects its adapter via the `model` param. --enable-lora and --lora-modules are all you need to start; dynamic load/unload via REST is available too.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** run a single vLLM server that hosts a shared base model and routes each request to a different fine-tuned LoRA adapter by name — no extra GPU required for each adapter.
- Load multiple LoRA adapters at launch with `--lora-modules`; clients select the adapter by passing its name in the `model` field - Control GPU residency with `--max-loras` and spill the rest to a CPU LRU cache for larger adapter pools - Add or remove adapters at runtime — no server restart — with the `/v1/load_lora_adapter` endpoint
**How it works.** The base model weights stay frozen and are computed once per batch. Each request also computes its LoRA delta weights (small — often 10–200 MB per adapter) which are then added to the base output. vLLM keeps up to `max_loras` adapters in GPU memory; others live in a CPU LRU cache and are paged in on demand.
**Start the server:**
```bash vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.2-8B-Instruct \ --enable-lora \ --max-loras 4 \ --max-lora-rank 64 \ --lora-modules \ '{"name":"sql-bot","path":"company/llama-sql-lora"}' \ '{"name":"support-bot","path":"company/llama-support-lora"}' ```
Set `--max-lora-rank` to match your highest-rank adapter exactly — setting it higher wastes GPU memory allocation.
**Route requests:**
```bash curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"sql-bot","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"List orders by date"}]}' ```
The base model is still reachable by its original model name.
**Dynamic load/unload (optional).** Set `VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=True`, then:
```bash # Load a new adapter without restarting curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/load_lora_adapter \ -d '{"lora_name":"new-adapter","lora_path":"/mnt/models/new-adapter"}' ```
**Where this breaks down.** Adapter switching adds ~2–5% per-request latency overhead for typical ranks. If nearly all traffic goes to one adapter, a dedicated server is cheaper. All adapters must share the same base model architecture — you cannot mix Llama and Mistral adapters on one server. High adapter diversity under load can cause LRU thrashing.
**Sources:** [vLLM LoRA Adapters docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/lora/), [vLLM multi-LoRA blog (Feb 2026)](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-02-26-multi-lora), [Spheron multi-adapter serving guide](https://www.spheron.network/blog/lora-multi-adapter-serving-gpu-cloud/), [Anyscale multi-LoRA docs](https://docs.anyscale.com/llm/serving/multi-lora)

item.title: Link Your Repo Before the First Prompt: What the Claude Design Export Bundle Hands Claude Code
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The handoff button bundles design files, chat history, and a README. Whether Claude Code lands your real components depends on one step done before the first prompt.
item.content:encoded:
**The Claude Design export bundles design files, chat history, and a README — but whether Claude Code lands your actual components depends on linking your codebase before you start.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** take a Claude Design prototype to code that uses your existing `Button`, `Card`, and `Modal` components — without a manual substitution pass.
**Three things that determine handoff quality:** - **A linked codebase gives Claude Design component-level context.** Without it, Claude Code writes Tailwind and generic HTML. With it, it generates calls to the components it already knows from your repo. - **Chat history is part of the bundle.** Every design decision you explained in conversation ("this header scrolls sticky on mobile") carries across to Claude Code. Write your constraints in chat, not just in the canvas. - **Names carry through.** If you called something "PricingCard" during the design conversation, that name appears in the handoff prompt. Naming elements clearly before Polish is free documentation for the handoff.
**Steps:**
1. **Connect your codebase first.** In Claude Design, click **Import** and connect your GitHub repo or a local directory. Claude reads your component library — this takes a few minutes and is what makes the next steps component-aware instead of generic.
2. **Design normally.** Claude now knows which `Tabs`, `Dialog`, and `Badge` components exist and generates the design using your existing ones rather than placeholders.
3. **Document your decisions in chat as you go.** When you make a choice ("the empty state shows after a 3-second delay, not on load"), say it in the chat. It enters the bundle and Claude Code inherits it.
4. **Export the bundle.** Click **Export → Hand off to Claude Code**. You get a URL and a ready-to-paste prompt.
5. **Paste into Claude Code.** The session fetches the bundle and begins implementing — editing existing components rather than generating from scratch.
**The failure mode independent practitioners report:** the handoff breaks down when designs lack component labels, loading states, and data assumptions. Claude Code inherits the ambiguity from the canvas, and pretty-but-underspecified designs become cleanup work rather than a running start. An extra five minutes on edge cases in the design conversation saves more than it costs.
One more limit: the bundle URL expires. Don't export on Friday and hand off Monday without checking whether it's still valid.
**Sources:** [Using Claude Design for prototypes and UX — Claude Academy](https://academy.claude.com/tutorials/using-claude-design-for-prototypes-and-ux) · [Set up your design system in Claude Design — Claude Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604397-set-up-your-design-system-in-claude-design) · [Claude Design doesn't fail in the canvas. It fails after export.](https://claudedesign.substack.com/p/the-claude-design-mistake-you-dont)

item.title: Three Agent SDK Settings That Prevent a Runaway Loop From Running All Night
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Set max_turns, max_budget_usd, and effort before deploying any Agent SDK loop — none have defaults, and an open-ended prompt without limits runs until the context window is exhausted.
item.content:encoded:
**Set `max_turns`, `max_budget_usd`, and `effort` before your first production Agent SDK call — none of them have defaults, and an open-ended prompt with no limits will run until context is exhausted.**
When you call `query()` in the Claude Agent SDK, the loop runs until Claude decides it's done. On a well-scoped task ("fix the failing test in auth.ts") that's usually a few turns. On an open-ended one ("improve this codebase") Claude will keep going until it hits a wall you didn't intend to set.
**`max_turns` / `maxTurns`** counts tool-use turns only (one round of Claude producing tool calls + the SDK executing them). A lint fix runs in 5–10 turns; a full-module refactor might need 30–50. When the limit is hit, `ResultMessage.subtype` is `"error_max_turns"` and `session_id` is preserved — you can resume with a higher limit rather than starting over.
**`max_budget_usd` / `maxBudgetUsd`** caps spend across the whole agent tree, including subagents. Once the budget is hit, Claude Code stops spawning further subagents and exits cleanly. Useful for batch jobs where you need predictable cost per item.
**`effort`** trades reasoning depth for cost. `"low"` for file lookups and directory scans; `"medium"` for routine edits; `"high"` for debugging or refactors; `"xhigh"` / `"max"` for deep multi-step analysis. Set it per subagent via `AgentDefinition.effort` to use cheap reasoning for search tasks and thorough reasoning for the synthesis step.
```python from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions
async for msg in query( prompt="Refactor the auth module and update all tests", options=ClaudeAgentOptions( allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Bash", "Glob", "Grep"], max_turns=40, max_budget_usd=0.50, effort="high", ), ): if msg.type == "result": print(f"Status: {msg.subtype}, Cost: ${msg.total_cost_usd:.4f}") ```
**Limit to know:** `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` have no defaults — if you don't set them, there's no automatic stop. An agent given `"improve this codebase"` without limits will run until the context window is exhausted. Also: `effort` is silently ignored on models that don't support it, so pin your model explicitly (`model="claude-sonnet-5"`) if you're relying on `effort` for cost control.
**Sources:** [How the agent loop works — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop) · [Context Window Management in AI Agents — Atlan (2026)](https://atlan.com/know/ai-agent/ai-agent-context/what-is-context-window-management-in-ai-agents/) · [Context Engineering for AI Agents — Sourcegraph](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/context-engineering)

item.title: Your RAG Pipeline Stores Vectors. Here's What Actually Searches Them: FAISS Explained
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: FAISS is Meta's in-memory C++ library for vector similarity search — the engine under most local RAG stacks. Three index types cover most use cases; persistence is a footgun you need to know about.
item.content:encoded:
**FAISS is Meta's pure in-memory C++ library for vector similarity search — the engine under most local RAG stacks. Three index types cover 95% of use cases; persistence requires an explicit save/load or you lose the index on process exit.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Use FAISS to build a searchable embedding index, pick the right index type for your dataset size, and understand what `Dataset.add_faiss_index()` is actually doing under the hood of a HuggingFace pipeline.
**Three things that clarify how FAISS works:**
- **FAISS does exactly one thing: find the k nearest vectors to a query.** It knows nothing about text, metadata, or persistence — it only handles arrays of float32. Everything else (chunking, embedding, metadata filtering) lives outside FAISS. Vector databases like Chroma, pgvector, and Qdrant manage all of that and offload the actual search step to FAISS or a similar ANN library internally.
- **Three index types cover most use cases.** `IndexFlatIP` (dot product) / `IndexFlatL2` (Euclidean) does exact brute-force search — 100% recall, but slow past ~500K vectors. `IndexIVFFlat` clusters vectors first with k-means and searches only the nearest clusters — 10–100× faster, with tunable recall via the `nprobe` parameter. `IndexHNSWFlat` uses a navigable graph — fast queries with high recall, but ~100 bytes/vector at M=32. For RAG prototypes under 500K chunks, Flat is fine. Past that, IVF first; HNSW when you need consistently high recall and can afford the RAM.
- **Persistence is not automatic.** FAISS lives entirely in RAM. `faiss.write_index(index, "my.index")` and `faiss.read_index("my.index")` are the only path to survive a process restart. This is FAISS's sharpest footgun.
**Hands-on: semantic search over GitHub issues (HuggingFace LLM Course, Chapter 5.6)**
```python from datasets import load_dataset from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1") ds = load_dataset("lewtun/github-issues", split="train")
# Embed a column and add the FAISS index in one pass ds = ds.map( lambda x: {"embeddings": model.encode(x["text"])}, batched=True, batch_size=32 ) ds.add_faiss_index(column="embeddings") # IndexFlatIP by default
# Query query_vec = model.encode("How do I install the library?") scores, results = ds.get_nearest_examples("embeddings", query_vec, k=5) for title in results["title"][:3]: print(title)
# Save and reload (required for production) ds.get_index("embeddings").save("github_issues.faiss") ds.load_faiss_index("embeddings", "github_issues.faiss") ```
**Where FAISS fits vs. a vector DB:** Use FAISS when you need pure speed on a dataset that fits in RAM and you don't need metadata filtering or persistence abstractions. Use Chroma, pgvector, or Qdrant when you need filters, multi-tenancy, or want persistence managed for you.
**Sources:** [Semantic search with FAISS — HuggingFace LLM Course Ch. 5.6](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter5/6) · [Vector Search with FAISS: ANN Explained — PyImageSearch (Feb 2026)](https://pyimagesearch.com/2026/02/16/vector-search-with-faiss-approximate-nearest-neighbor-ann-explained/) · [FAISS library — Facebook Research GitHub](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss)

item.title: Add and Remove Tools Between Agent Turns Without Blowing Up Your Cache
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The mid-conversation-tool-changes-2026-07-01 beta lets you offer or withdraw tools at any point in a conversation without editing the tools array — the cached prefix stays intact.
item.content:encoded:
**Declare all tools up front, then use `tool_addition`/`tool_removal` content blocks in a `role: "system"` message to surface or withdraw tools mid-session — the `tools` array never changes, so the cached prefix stays intact.**
Multi-step agent workflows often need different tools at different phases: a planning pass that can call `search` and `read_file`; an execution pass that can call `bash` but not `search`. The old choice was fix the tool list for the session (simple, inflexible) or edit the `tools` array between turns (flexible, but invalidates the entire cache every time). Mid-conversation tool changes give you a third path.
**How it works:**
1. Declare every tool in the top-level `tools` array at session start. Tools you want withheld initially: set `defer_loading: true`. 2. When the conversation reaches the point where a tool becomes relevant, inject a `role: "system"` message with a `tool_addition` content block naming the tool. 3. To withdraw a tool, inject a `tool_removal` block the same way.
```python import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic()
response = client.beta.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=2048, betas=["mid-conversation-tool-changes-2026-07-01"], tools=[ { "name": "bash", "description": "Run shell commands.", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"command": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["command"]}, "defer_loading": True, # withheld at session start }, { "name": "search", "description": "Search the web.", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"]}, }, ], messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "Research this topic, then write a script to process the results."}, # ... planning turns with search active ... # Transition: withdraw search, surface bash { "role": "system", "content": [ {"type": "tool_removal", "tool": {"type": "tool_reference", "name": "search"}}, {"type": "tool_addition", "tool": {"type": "tool_reference", "name": "bash"}}, ], }, # Execution turns: bash available, search withdrawn ], ) ```
**Key limits before shipping:** - **Beta header required:** `anthropic-beta: mid-conversation-tool-changes-2026-07-01`. Available on Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5. **Not available on Sonnet 5** — use the static top-level `tools` array there. - **Reference only, never define mid-session:** `tool_addition`/`tool_removal` blocks name a tool from the session's `tools` array. A name not declared there returns a 400 immediately. - **MCP toolsets supported:** reference an entire MCP server's toolset with `mcp_toolset_reference` and a `server_name` to add or remove the whole set in one block.
The technique pairs naturally with `defer_loading: true` — pre-register every tool at session start, withhold the dangerous or phase-inappropriate ones, surface them only when the conversation state justifies it.
**Sources:** [Mid-conversation system messages and tool changes — Anthropic Platform Docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages) · [Claude API Now Lets You Change Tools Mid-Conversation — BlurBrahLab via Medium](https://blurbrahlab.medium.com/claude-api-now-lets-you-change-tools-mid-conversation-without-breaking-the-cache-top-10-ai-4c30954c4be7) · [Claude API: Swap Tools Mid-Session Without Cache Blowup — ByteIota](https://byteiota.com/claude-api-swap-tools-mid-session-without-cache-blowup/)

item.title: RAG Handles Facts That Change; Fine-Tuning Handles Behavior That Shouldn't — Here Is the Decision Tree
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: When to retrieve vs. when to train: a five-question decision tree that routes LLM problems to the right approach — and the production hybrid pattern that combines both without wasting either.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** decide whether your LLM problem calls for RAG, fine-tuning, or the specific combination that survives a base-model upgrade — before you've written a line of training code.
RAG and fine-tuning solve different problems. Choosing wrong doesn't make the system fail outright — it makes it expensive to maintain, brittle when the base model upgrades, and hard to improve.
**Three-bullet takeaway:** - RAG is for knowledge that changes. Fine-tuning is for behavior that shouldn't. When in doubt, RAG is cheaper to start and easier to discard. - The strongest fine-tuning case in 2026 is distillation: training a small model to match a frontier model's quality on your specific task at around one-tenth the inference cost. - The production hybrid is not "both at once." It is: build a RAG baseline, run it, collect the failure cases retrieval cannot fix, then fine-tune a small adapter on exactly those residuals.
**The decision tree — walk it in order:**
**1. Does the answer depend on data that changes?** -> RAG. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights and goes stale when data updates. You cannot fine-tune something you would have to retrain weekly.
**2. Do you need source citations or an audit trail?** -> RAG. A fine-tuned model cannot point to the document it drew from. RAG returns documents alongside the answer.
**3. Do you need a fixed output schema or deeply consistent tone?** -> Fine-tune. Per Winder AI's framework, prompting alone cannot lock output structure reliably at scale; a thin LoRA adapter on a smaller model is cheaper to serve and more consistent than a frontier model on a long prompt.
**4. Is inference cost or latency a hard constraint?** -> Fine-tune for distillation. A QLoRA-distilled 8B model can match a frontier model on a narrow task at about one-tenth the per-token rate, according to Winder AI's 2026 benchmarks — the commercial case most teams discover last.
**5. Otherwise?** -> Start with RAG, measure, then revisit fine-tuning for gaps retrieval cannot close.
**The production hybrid pattern:** Build the RAG baseline and run it. Collect the queries where retrieval still fails — wrong chunks, hallucinated answers, inconsistent format. That failure set is the fine-tuning dataset. Train a small adapter on it. The result: live facts from retrieval, locked behavior from fine-tuning, inference on a model small enough to keep costs predictable.
**The real constraint to know:** fine-tuning couples you to a specific base model version. When the model lab ships an upgrade, your adapter typically needs retraining from scratch. RAG survives a base-model swap with nothing more than a re-embedding run and a re-index.
**One resource to anchor this:** [Is Fine-Tuning Still Needed? LLMs, RAG, & LoRA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-W2JdSl1v48) — a 30-minute video that covers the mechanics of both approaches and walks through the decision points with worked examples. Follow it with the written decision framework below for the 2026 production angle.
**Sources:** [RAG vs Fine-Tuning 2026: A Decision Framework — Winder.AI](https://winder.ai/rag-vs-fine-tuning-2026-decision-framework/) · [Is Fine-Tuning Still Needed? LLMs, RAG, & LoRA — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-W2JdSl1v48) · [RAG vs Fine-Tuning for LLMs — HuggingFace Blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/airabbitX/rag-vs-fine-tuning-for-llms-a-com)

item.title: Point --plugin-dir at a Folder and Claude Code 2.1.265 Auto-Loads Every Plugin Inside It
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code 2.1.265: --plugin-dir now accepts a parent directory — every subfolder with a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest auto-loads. One flag, your whole team plugin suite.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code 2.1.265 (September 8): `--plugin-dir` now accepts a parent folder — every subfolder with a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest auto-loads in one flag.**
Before 2.1.265, `--plugin-dir` pointed at a single plugin directory. Loading multiple plugins meant multiple flags, or a wrapper script that assembled the list. The update changes that: point `--plugin-dir` at a parent directory and Claude Code scans one level deep, auto-loading every immediate subdirectory that contains a valid plugin manifest.
Structure a shared plugin collection like this:
``` my-org-plugins/ api-checker/ .claude-plugin/plugin.json # skills + hooks for checking internal APIs github-tools/ .claude-plugin/plugin.json # custom gh commands the team has standardized style-enforcer/ .claude-plugin/plugin.json # hooks to enforce your coding style ```
Then load the whole suite with one flag:
```bash claude --plugin-dir ~/my-org-plugins/ ```
To make it the default for everyone who opens a project, add it to the repo's `.claude/settings.json`:
```json { "pluginDirs": ["~/my-org-plugins/"] } ```
Use `/reload-plugins` inside a session to pick up plugin changes without restarting.
**Where it breaks:** The directory scan is one level deep — nested plugin directories do not auto-load. A local `--plugin-dir` plugin shadows any same-named marketplace plugin for that session, which is useful for testing changes but easy to forget when a teammate reports different behavior. The flag also accepts a `.zip` archive of the plugin directory if you want to distribute the collection as a single file.
**Sources:** [Claude Code 2.1.265 changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Claude Code plugins documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins) · [Awesome Claude Plugins community list](https://github.com/composio-community/awesome-claude-plugins)

item.title: 207 GPU Kernels, No Server Required — @huggingface/kernels Brings ML Ops to Your Users' Browsers
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: HuggingFace shipped @huggingface/kernels (Sept 1): 207 WebGPU ML operations via npm. Run attention and matmul in your users' browsers — no server endpoint needed.
item.content:encoded:
**HuggingFace's new `@huggingface/kernels` puts 207 WebGPU-optimized ML operations in your npm install — no server endpoint needed for embedding generation or lightweight inference.**
HuggingFace's Web AI team shipped `@huggingface/kernels` on September 1: 207 GPU operations (attention, matrix multiplication, layernorm, activations) that run in the browser via WebGPU. Instead of adding a server endpoint for an embedding call, you load a kernel and pass typed tensors:
```js import { getKernel } from "@huggingface/kernels"; const matmul = await getKernel("huggingface/kernels-matmul-wgsl", { rev: "v0.1" }); const result = await matmul(a, b, shape); ```
Each kernel ships with correctness test cases, performance benchmarks, and parameterized WGSL shader implementations as versioned Hub packages. The library includes Fleet, an in-browser GPU benchmarking tool that scores kernels on your specific hardware before you build on them.
**Where it breaks:** WebGPU support varies — Safari's implementation is partial, and the library is preview-tagged for a reason: HuggingFace documents that 947 of the 1,756 ORT WebGPU reference test cases produced unreliable results. Benchmarks measure individual GPU operations only, not full model inference (shader compilation and data transfer add latency on top).
**Why it matters:** If you are adding embedding generation or a lightweight classifier to a web app, this is worth evaluating as an alternative to a server round-trip. For anything requiring a full model pipeline, the coverage gaps mean server inference remains more reliable.
**Sources:** [HuggingFace @huggingface/kernels blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/webgpu-kernels) · [WebGPU Kernels: Local AI Closer to the Browser — Ken Ashe](https://kenashe.ai/blog/2026-09-01-webgpu-kernels-move-local-ai-closer-to-the-browser) · [HuggingFace ships 207 Apache-2.0 WebGPU kernels](https://ccleaks.com/news/huggingface-webgpu-kernels-sep-2026)

item.title: Your Brand Colors Live in Your Head, Not Claude Code's — Structure a tokens.json File It Can Actually Read
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Give Claude Code a W3C DTCG tokens.json file and it uses your actual brand colors and spacing — not generic defaults — from the first component it generates.
item.content:encoded:
**Give Claude Code a W3C DTCG tokens.json file and it uses your actual brand colors and spacing — not generic defaults — from the first component it generates.**
When Claude Code generates a component, it defaults to whatever spacing and colors make sense to it — typically Bootstrap-adjacent values (16px gaps, generic blues). That is not incompetence; it just does not know your system exists.
The fix is a `tokens.json` file in the [W3C Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG) format](https://www.designtokens.org/tr/drafts/format/) — the spec backed by Figma, Adobe, Google, and Shopify, that every serious design-to-code tool now reads and writes. The shape is simple: each token has a `$value` and a `$type`.
```json { "color": { "brand": { "primary": { "$value": "#3b82f6", "$type": "color" }, "surface": { "$value": "#0f172a", "$type": "color" } } }, "spacing": { "md": { "$value": "16px", "$type": "dimension" }, "lg": { "$value": "24px", "$type": "dimension" } } } ```
Reference it in your `CLAUDE.md`:
```markdown ## Design system All color and spacing values are in `tokens.json` (W3C DTCG format). Use `color.brand.primary.$value` for primary actions, `color.brand.surface.$value` for page backgrounds. Do not invent values — look them up in the token file. ```
Then run [Style Dictionary v4](https://styledictionary.com/info/dtcg/) to generate CSS custom properties, Tailwind config, and TypeScript constants from the same source:
```bash npx style-dictionary build --config sd.config.mjs ```
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Claude Code generates components that start from your palette, and the same `tokens.json` drives both the agent instructions and your CSS output.
**Three-bullet takeaway:** - The DTCG 2025.10 spec defines the portable JSON shape: `$value`/`$type` per token, with alias references via `{path.to.token}` for semantic token trees. - Style Dictionary v4 processes DTCG tokens into CSS vars, Tailwind config, or TS constants in one command — one source file, many output formats. - The gap: Claude Code respects the token file when CLAUDE.md points to it, but for multi-component sessions you still benefit from explicit references in your prompts ("use the `color.brand.primary` token, not a hardcoded hex").
**Sources:** [Design Tokens Community Group spec 2025.10](https://www.designtokens.org/tr/drafts/format/) · [Style Dictionary DTCG support docs](https://styledictionary.com/info/dtcg/) · [W3C announcement: specification reaches first stable version](https://www.w3.org/community/design-tokens/2025/10/28/design-tokens-specification-reaches-first-stable-version/) · [W3C DTCG practical guide](https://tasteprofile.io/blog/w3c-dtcg-design-tokens-practical-guide)

item.title: Claude Code Has Been Taking Notes About Your Project in a File You've Probably Never Opened
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code's auto memory writes session notes to ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md — the first 200 lines load every session. Here's how to read, curate, and fix stale entries.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code writes cross-session notes about your project to `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md` — the first 200 lines load on every new session, so the quality of that file matters.**
Every time Claude corrects a mistake you flag, discovers your build command, or learns a debugging pattern that consistently works in your project, it optionally saves a note. These accumulate in a `MEMORY.md` index file — loaded at the start of the next session before you type anything.
**Browse what it saved:** ```bash # From within a session: /memory # opens the memory directory browser
# Or directly in the shell: cat ~/.claude/projects/*/memory/MEMORY.md ```
The directory also holds per-topic files — `feedback_testing.md`, `user_role.md`, and any others Claude creates. `MEMORY.md` acts as an index; Claude loads it at session start and reads the topic files on demand as it needs them. The limit is the first 200 lines or 25KB of `MEMORY.md`, whichever comes first — everything past that threshold is silently dropped on load.
**Four note types Claude saves:** - `user` — your role and working preferences - `feedback` — corrections you've given and approaches you confirmed work - `project` — ongoing work, decisions, and context Claude can't derive from the code - `reference` — external resources like your issue tracker or dashboard URL
Claude skips anything it can derive from the codebase itself: architecture, file paths, debugging patterns visible in the code. It also doesn't save something every session — only when the information would be useful in a future conversation.
**Monthly audit pattern:** ```bash # Review the index cat ~/.claude/projects/*/memory/MEMORY.md
# Edit stale entries directly $EDITOR ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md ```
**The contamination failure mode:** auto memory is per-repository, shared across all worktrees. If you've been on a long-running feature branch, `MEMORY.md` can accumulate contradictory facts — "the payment module uses the v1 API" from last sprint alongside "use the v2 payment API" from this one. Both load every session and both shape Claude's context. A quarterly audit that removes facts about removed dependencies and finished features is the fix.
**Machine-local, not cloud-synced:** auto memory is per-machine. Cloud and remote sessions write to their own separate memory directories and never sync back to your local machine. If you rely on remote execution heavily, check what each environment has accumulated independently.
**To disable for a project:** ```json // .claude/settings.json { "autoMemoryEnabled": false } ``` Or set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` for a single session.
**Sources:** [Claude Code memory docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) · [Automatic Memory Is Not Learning — Medium/@brentwpeterson](https://medium.com/@brentwpeterson/automatic-memory-is-not-learning-4191f548df4c) · [Claude Code Memory Persistence Guide — thepromptshelf.dev](https://thepromptshelf.dev/blog/claude-code-memory-persistence-guide-2026/)

item.title: 'Budget Flights' Should Find 'Cheap Tickets' — Here's the Embedding Pipeline That Makes It Happen
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Dense vector embeddings let you match meaning, not keywords. sentence-transformers generates them in three lines — this is the layer every RAG pipeline and vector database tutorial starts from.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** generate dense vector embeddings from any text, score semantic similarity with cosine to find paraphrases that keyword search misses, and understand why every RAG pipeline starts here before the index.
Keyword search matches tokens. A query for "budget flights" misses a document that says "cheap tickets to Heathrow" — no shared terms, no result. Dense embeddings sidestep this by encoding meaning into a float vector, where similar concepts cluster near each other regardless of wording.
**Three-line version:** ```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") embeddings = model.encode(["cheap tickets", "budget aviation", "quantum entanglement"]) print(model.similarity(embeddings[0:1], embeddings)) # → [[1.0, 0.82, 0.15]] ```
`all-MiniLM-L6-v2` maps each input to a 384-dimension float vector. Cosine similarity — the dot product of L2-normalized vectors — gives a score from −1 to 1. "Cheap tickets" and "budget aviation" score 0.82; "quantum entanglement" scores 0.15.
**Three starting model choices:**
| Model | Params | Dims | When to use | |---|---|---|---| | `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` | 22M | 384 | Fast, CPU-friendly, good enough for most RAG | | `all-mpnet-base-v2` | 110M | 768 | Better quality, ~3× slower | | OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` | — | 1536 | No local GPU, managed scale |
**The one limit that bites before you go further:** sentence-transformers silently truncates input at the model's max sequence length — typically 512 tokens — with no warning. A 2,000-word document gets its tail dropped: the last ~75% of a long document disappears. For anything longer than a short paragraph, chunk first, embed each chunk, and store them as separate vectors. This is why every RAG chunking step comes before embedding, not after.
**3-bullet takeaway:** - `SentenceTransformer.encode()` → float vector, `model.similarity()` → cosine score; that's the full retrieval API for a first-pass semantic search - `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is the right default until your recall numbers say otherwise - Silent 512-token truncation is the gotcha that causes retrieval misses on long documents — chunk first
**Why this matters for what you build:** when you call `ChromaDB.add()`, `pgvector`'s INSERT, or LangChain's `HuggingFaceBgeEmbeddings.embed_documents()`, one of these models runs under the hood. Knowing what it produces — and where it truncates — is the foundation for diagnosing retrieval misses when your search returns the wrong chunks.
**Sources:** [sentence-transformers quickstart — sbert.net](https://sbert.net/docs/quickstart.html) · [Semantic Search docs — sbert.net](https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/semantic-search/README.html) · [An Intuitive Explanation of Sentence-BERT — Towards Data Science](https://towardsdatascience.com/an-intuitive-explanation-of-sentence-bert-1984d144a868/)

item.title: Your Parallel Claude Code Sessions Can Now Coordinate Without You in the Middle
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.224 adds cross-session messaging: two independent sessions on the same machine can pass findings and decisions directly via ListAgents + SendMessage, no copy-paste required.
item.content:encoded:
**Since v2.1.224 (August 7), Claude Code sessions on the same machine can message each other. `ListAgents` discovers which sessions are running; `SendMessage` delivers. The practical win: parallel sessions pass findings and decisions without you copy-pasting between terminals.**
When you run two Claude Code sessions in parallel — one on a backend schema migration, one on the API layer that depends on it — the natural breakpoint is when one session has a finding the other needs. Before cross-session messaging, you stopped, copied the relevant context, and re-explained it. Now Claude routes it.
**How it works.** Two tools power it: `ListAgents` and `SendMessage`. You never call them yourself — Claude discovers the target and composes the message from your prompt.
The simplest form: ``` Let @api-worker know the schema migration finished and tenant_id is the new column ``` Claude finds the session named `api-worker` and writes the message. The receiving session shows a preview and Claude reads the full text.
You can also ask Claude to poll another session: ``` Ask the session in my other terminal whether the migration is done yet ``` Or subscribe to a one-shot notification when a long-running task finishes: ``` Tell me when the migration session finishes what it's working on ``` That last form sends one notice the next time the watched session goes idle — no polling, no repeated messages.
**Session naming.** Type `/list-agents` (or `/peers`) to see every session Claude can reach. Use `--name <name>` at launch or `/rename` mid-session to make sessions easy to @-mention.
**Limits to know:** - **Text only.** No conversation history, no files, no structured tool calls cross session boundaries. The size cap is about 1M characters. - **Same machine only** without Remote Control. Reaching sessions on another machine requires a Remote Control connection. - **A received message cannot approve pending permission prompts** or change settings in the receiving session — it is not treated as your input. - Rapid bursts to one session are throttled automatically; identical repeat messages within a short window are dropped.
Available on macOS and Linux (including WSL2) from v2.1.224; native Windows from v2.1.234.

item.title: Tencent's Hy4 Opens Up the First 1M-Context Open-Weight Model — Self-Hosting Needs a Datacenter
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Tencent's Hy4 Preview (770B/49B-active MoE, Apache 2.0) is the first open-weight model with a 1M-token context. Self-hosting needs 8 B300 GPUs; OpenRouter is the practical entry point.
item.content:encoded:
**Tencent's Hy4 Preview is a 770B-total/49B-active-per-token Mixture-of-Experts model released on HuggingFace August 28 under Apache 2.0, with a genuine 1M-token context window — the first open-weight model to credibly offer this at commercial scale.**
The architecture is 78 transformer layers, each with 256 routed experts plus one shared expert; each token activates the top 8 routed experts plus the shared one. On coding benchmarks, Tencent reports 65.7 on SWE-bench Pro and 64.3 on DeepSWE (comparable to closed frontier models, per Tencent's own evaluation). An independent practitioner review by Wavect found it retained "requirements, implementation state, and tool outputs" well across longer agentic workflows.
**The practical ceiling is hardware.** Tencent's own deployment recipes require at minimum 8 NVIDIA B300 GPUs (or 16 B200s) for the BF16 variant under vLLM with 8-way tensor parallelism; an FP8 quantized variant lowers that but remains datacenter-class. Prebuilt containers (`vllm/vllm-openai:hy4-preview`, `lmsysorg/sglang:hy4-preview`) are available for both. For most teams, OpenRouter (Tencent reports $0.83/M input, $2.50/M output) or WorkBuddy is the practical entry point — not self-hosting.
**Two limits before committing.** Independent testing found that 1M-token context ≠ 1M-token recall: accuracy degrades as the context window fills, same as all other long-context models. The model also has a documented tendency to over-verify on complex tasks, generating unnecessary reasoning steps that drive up cost.
**Why it matters:** If your agent pipeline is hitting a ceiling on long repository retrieval or multi-document reasoning, Hy4 is the first open-weight option that competes with closed frontier models on context length — with an Apache 2.0 license that carries none of the community-agreement restrictions on the Llama line.
**Sources:** [TechNode Global](https://technode.global/2026/09/04/tencent-hy4-preview-open-source-model/) · [Independent review — Wavect.io](https://wavect.io/blog/tencent-hy4-preview-coding-agent-review/) · [BenchLM independent benchmarks](https://benchlm.ai/models/hy4-preview) · [Forbes coverage (Aug 31)](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jonmarkman/2026/08/31/tencent-open-sources-hy4-its-770-billion-parameter-flagship-model/)

item.title: HuggingFace: A 350M Model Learns Structured Output Compliance in 100 GRPO Steps
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: HuggingFace's September 3 guide fine-tunes LFM2.5-350M with GRPO+TRL+LoRA on 500 examples in 100 steps, raising IFStruct structured-output accuracy from 22.6% to 29.7% — runs on a free Colab GPU.
item.content:encoded:
**A September 3 HuggingFace guide shows GRPO fine-tuning a 350M-parameter model on 500 examples in 100 steps — per the IFStruct benchmark, structured output accuracy rises from 22.6% to 29.7% on a free Colab GPU.**
A September 3 HuggingFace post fine-tunes LiquidAI's LFM2.5-350M using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) with TRL and LoRA adapters — only 6M of the model's 350M parameters are updated. Training data: 500 examples. Steps: 100. Hardware: free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU. Per the IFStruct benchmark, schema-adherence accuracy goes from 22.6% to 29.7%, with JSON compliance driving most of the gain: +13.9 points on JSON-specific tasks.
The technique works because GRPO uses a verifiable pass/fail reward — valid JSON parses, invalid JSON doesn't — so it doesn't need preference labels or a reward model. The reward function is your schema validator.
**Why it matters for agents:** Local models that drop malformed JSON on 15–20% of turns will interrupt any agentic pipeline that calls tool APIs. 100 GRPO training steps against a JSON schema validator may be the fastest fix — cheaper than switching to a larger model, and cheaper than adding retry logic that obscures the underlying problem.
**Two limits worth knowing:** YAML compliance barely moved (+0.3 points per the same benchmark) despite JSON improving significantly — GRPO's reward needs a reliable verifiable signal, and YAML parsers are strict about whitespace in ways that weaken it. Also, 29.7% still trails Qwen3.5-2B (33.15%) on IFStruct, per the post's own comparison — evaluate before committing to fine-tuning over simply choosing a more capable model.
**Sources:** [Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps — HuggingFace Blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/grpo-with-trl-ifstruct) · [GRPO Trainer — TRL docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/grpo_trainer) · [GRPO — DeepSeek-R1, arXiv:2501.12948](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)
